title: Anatomy & Physiology
description: Free Anatomy & Physiology study guide: 8 units, 320 practice questions, 80 flashcards, quick reference, memory tricks, and a full practice exam. Completely free.

units.name: Intro & Terminology

concepts.intro: Standard anatomical position (standing, facing forward, arms at sides, palms forward) is the reference point for all directional terminology in anatomy.
b: Superior (toward the head) vs inferior (toward the feet)
Anterior/ventral (front) vs posterior/dorsal (back)
Medial (toward the midline) vs lateral (away from the midline)
Proximal (closer to trunk) vs distal (farther from trunk), used for limbs
Superficial (near the surface) vs deep (farther from the surface)
Palms face forward in anatomical position, not at the sides as in a relaxed stance

concepts.intro: Planes are imaginary flat surfaces used to describe cuts or views through the body.
b: Sagittal plane divides the body into left and right parts
Midsagittal (median) plane creates exactly equal left and right halves
Frontal (coronal) plane divides the body into anterior and posterior parts
Transverse (horizontal/axial) plane divides the body into superior and inferior parts
CT and MRI scans are typically read as transverse sections

concepts.intro: The body's internal organs are housed in cavities lined by protective membranes.
b: Dorsal cavity contains the cranial cavity (brain) and vertebral canal (spinal cord)
Ventral cavity contains the thoracic cavity and abdominopelvic cavity
The diaphragm separates the thoracic cavity from the abdominopelvic cavity
Thoracic cavity contains two pleural cavities (lungs) and the mediastinum (heart, esophagus, trachea)
Serous membranes (pleura, pericardium, peritoneum) reduce friction with a thin fluid layer between parietal and visceral layers

concepts.intro: Anatomy studies structure at increasing levels of complexity, from atoms to the whole organism.
b: Chemical level: atoms combine into molecules (e.g., DNA, proteins)
Cellular level: the basic structural and functional unit of life
Tissue level: groups of similar cells performing a common function
Organ level: two or more tissue types working together (e.g., the heart)
Organ system level: organs working together for a common purpose (e.g., cardiovascular system)
Organismal level: all systems functioning together as a whole living being

concepts.intro: Homeostasis is the body's ability to maintain a stable internal environment despite external changes.
b: Negative feedback loops reverse a change and are the most common regulatory mechanism (e.g., blood glucose regulation by insulin)
Positive feedback loops amplify a change until a specific endpoint is reached (e.g., labor contractions via oxytocin)
A feedback loop has three components: receptor (detects stimulus), control center (processes information), and effector (produces the response)
Failure of homeostatic control contributes to disease states

concepts.intro: All organs are built from combinations of four basic tissue types, each with a distinct structure and function.
b: Epithelial tissue covers body surfaces and lines cavities/organs; it is avascular and regenerates quickly
Connective tissue supports, binds, and protects (e.g., bone, cartilage, blood, adipose tissue)
Muscle tissue contracts to produce movement (skeletal, cardiac, smooth)
Nervous tissue generates and transmits electrical impulses (neurons and neuroglia)

keyFacts: Anatomical position always assumes palms facing forward, regardless of the body's actual posture
The abdominopelvic cavity is often divided into 9 regions or 4 quadrants for clinical description
Anatomy studies structure while physiology studies function — the two are inseparable in practice
Negative feedback maintains stability; positive feedback drives a process to completion, then stops
traps: 'Anterior' and 'ventral' are synonyms in humans, not opposites
A sagittal cut does not have to be down the midline — only the midsagittal plane splits the body into exact mirror halves
The stomach is an organ, not a tissue — it is made of all four tissue types working together
Positive feedback is not 'bad'; it is a normal, self-limiting mechanism (e.g., childbirth, blood clotting), not a runaway malfunction

units.name: Skeletal System

concepts.intro: Bones are classified by shape and built from distinct tissue layers that combine strength with light weight.
b: Long bones (femur, humerus) have a diaphysis (shaft) and epiphyses (ends)
Short bones (carpals, tarsals) are roughly cube-shaped and provide stability with limited motion
Flat bones (skull, sternum, scapula) protect organs and provide broad muscle attachment surfaces
Irregular bones (vertebrae, facial bones) have complex shapes that fit specific functions
Compact bone forms the dense outer layer; spongy (cancellous) bone forms the lighter, porous interior
The medullary cavity of long bones stores yellow bone marrow (fat) in adults

concepts.intro: The axial skeleton forms the body's central axis and protects the brain, spinal cord, and thoracic organs.
b: The skull consists of 8 cranial bones and 14 facial bones
The vertebral column has 33 vertebrae grouped as 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 fused sacral, and 4 fused coccygeal
The rib cage includes 12 pairs of ribs, the sternum, and thoracic vertebrae
True ribs (1-7) attach directly to the sternum via costal cartilage; false ribs (8-12) do not attach directly
The hyoid bone is unique because it does not articulate with any other bone

concepts.intro: The appendicular skeleton includes the limbs and the girdles that attach them to the axial skeleton, enabling movement.
b: The pectoral (shoulder) girdle consists of the clavicle and scapula
The upper limb includes the humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, metacarpals, and phalanges
The pelvic girdle consists of the fused hip bones (ilium, ischium, pubis), which attach to the sacrum
The lower limb includes the femur, patella, tibia, fibula, tarsals, metatarsals, and phalanges
The femur is the longest and strongest bone in the human body

concepts.intro: Joints are classified by the tissue connecting the bones and by the degree of movement they allow.
b: Fibrous joints (e.g., skull sutures) are immovable (synarthroses)
Cartilaginous joints (e.g., between vertebrae, pubic symphysis) allow slight movement (amphiarthroses)
Synovial joints (e.g., knee, shoulder) are freely movable (diarthroses) and contain synovial fluid within a joint capsule
Types of synovial joints include hinge (elbow, knee), ball-and-socket (shoulder, hip), pivot (atlas-axis), and saddle (thumb)
Ligaments connect bone to bone and stabilize joints

concepts.intro: Bone is a dynamic, living tissue that grows, remodels, and heals throughout life through the coordinated action of specialized cells.
b: Osteoblasts build new bone matrix; osteocytes maintain mature bone; osteoclasts break down (resorb) bone tissue
Longitudinal (lengthwise) bone growth occurs at the epiphyseal plate (growth plate) during childhood and adolescence
Ossification (osteogenesis) is the process of bone formation, occurring via intramembranous (flat bones) or endochondral (most other bones) pathways
Bone remodeling continuously replaces old bone tissue in response to mechanical stress and calcium needs
Fracture repair proceeds through a hematoma, fibrocartilaginous callus, bony callus, and final remodeling

concepts.intro: Beyond providing structure, the skeleton performs critical physiological roles and is subject to specific pathologies.
b: Functions include support, protection, movement (via muscle attachment), mineral storage (calcium, phosphorus), and blood cell formation (hematopoiesis in red marrow)
Osteoporosis is a decrease in bone density/mass that increases fracture risk, common in postmenopausal women due to lower estrogen
Osteoarthritis involves the breakdown of articular cartilage at joints, causing pain and stiffness
Rickets (children) and osteomalacia (adults) result from vitamin D deficiency causing softened bones
Scoliosis is an abnormal lateral curvature of the spine

keyFacts: The adult human skeleton has 206 bones total: 80 axial and 126 appendicular
Red bone marrow (found in flat bones and epiphyses) produces blood cells; yellow bone marrow stores fat
The femur is both the longest and strongest bone; the stapes (in the ear) is the smallest
Calcium and phosphate ions give bone its hardness, while collagen fibers give it flexibility and resistance to fracture
traps: Cartilage is not bone — cartilage lacks blood vessels and calcified matrix, while bone is highly vascularized and mineralized
The epiphyseal plate is cartilage, not bone, until it fully ossifies (closes) after puberty, ending height growth
Ligaments connect bone to bone; tendons connect muscle to bone — these are commonly reversed by students
Not all joints are synovial (freely movable) — sutures of the skull are fibrous and immovable, not 'stiff synovial joints'

units.name: Muscular System

concepts.intro: The body contains three distinct types of muscle tissue, each suited to a specific function and control mechanism.
b: Skeletal muscle is voluntary, striated, and multinucleated; it attaches to bone via tendons
Cardiac muscle is involuntary, striated, and found only in the heart; cells are connected by intercalated discs
Smooth muscle is involuntary, non-striated, and lines hollow organs (intestines, blood vessels, bladder)
Intercalated discs contain gap junctions that allow electrical signals to spread rapidly between cardiac cells
Skeletal muscle fibers are multinucleated because they form from the fusion of many myoblasts during development

concepts.intro: Skeletal muscle is organized hierarchically from whole muscle down to the contractile proteins that generate force.
b: A muscle is made of fascicles, which are bundles of individual muscle fibers (cells)
Each muscle fiber contains many myofibrils, composed of repeating sarcomeres
The sarcomere is the basic functional contractile unit, bounded by Z-discs
Thick filaments are made of myosin; thin filaments are made of actin
The sarcoplasmic reticulum stores calcium ions needed for muscle contraction
Connective tissue wrappings include the epimysium (whole muscle), perimysium (fascicles), and endomysium (individual fibers)

concepts.intro: Muscle contraction occurs when thin filaments slide past thick filaments, shortening the sarcomere without the filaments themselves changing length.
b: A nerve impulse triggers acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction
Acetylcholine binding causes depolarization and release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Calcium binds troponin, shifting tropomyosin to expose myosin-binding sites on actin
Myosin heads bind actin, forming cross-bridges and pulling thin filaments toward the sarcomere's center (power stroke)
ATP is required to detach myosin from actin, allowing the cycle to repeat or the muscle to relax
During contraction, the H zone and I band narrow, but the A band length stays the same

concepts.intro: Muscles generate ATP through multiple pathways depending on the intensity and duration of activity.
b: The phosphocreatine system provides immediate, short-term ATP for the first ~10-15 seconds of intense activity
Anaerobic glycolysis produces ATP quickly without oxygen but yields lactic acid as a byproduct, useful for short bursts
Aerobic (cellular) respiration produces the most ATP but requires oxygen and is used during sustained, lower-intensity activity
Muscle fatigue results from ATP depletion, lactic acid accumulation, and ion imbalances
Slow-twitch (Type I) fibers are fatigue-resistant and rely on aerobic metabolism; fast-twitch (Type II) fibers fatigue quickly but generate more power

concepts.intro: Muscles work in coordinated groups, and their names often describe their location, shape, or action.
b: The prime mover (agonist) is the main muscle producing a movement; the antagonist opposes/reverses it
Synergists assist the prime mover; fixators stabilize the origin bone so force is applied effectively
The origin is the fixed attachment point; the insertion is the movable attachment point that moves toward the origin during contraction
Muscle naming conventions include location (biceps brachii), shape (deltoid = triangular), size (maximus/minimus), and number of origins (biceps = two heads)
Isotonic contractions change muscle length (concentric = shortening, eccentric = lengthening); isometric contractions produce tension without changing length

concepts.intro: Understanding major superficial muscles and common muscular disorders connects structure to real-world function and pathology.
b: Major muscles include the biceps brachii/triceps brachii (elbow flexion/extension), quadriceps/hamstrings (knee extension/flexion), deltoid (shoulder abduction), and gastrocnemius (plantarflexion)
The diaphragm is the primary muscle of respiration
Muscular dystrophy is a group of genetic disorders causing progressive muscle weakness and degeneration
Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disease that attacks acetylcholine receptors, causing muscle weakness and fatigue
Tetanus (the sustained contraction, not the disease) occurs when stimulation frequency is high enough that the muscle cannot relax between twitches

keyFacts: There are over 600 skeletal muscles in the human body, making up roughly 40% of body mass
ATP is required for both contraction (myosin head movement) and relaxation (detaching myosin from actin)
Calcium is the trigger that couples nervous stimulation to physical contraction (excitation-contraction coupling)
Cardiac muscle is involuntary and self-exciting (autorhythmic), unlike skeletal muscle which requires nervous stimulation to contract
traps: Muscles only pull, they never push — movement in the opposite direction requires an antagonist muscle, not the same muscle reversing
Rigor mortis occurs because of a LACK of ATP after death, preventing myosin from detaching from actin — not from excess calcium alone
The sarcomere shortens during contraction, but the individual thick and thin filaments do NOT shorten — they slide past each other
'Muscle tone' refers to a constant, low-level partial contraction at rest, not muscle size or strength

units.name: Nervous System

concepts.intro: Neurons are the specialized cells that generate and transmit electrical and chemical signals throughout the nervous system.
b: Dendrites receive incoming signals and conduct them toward the cell body
The cell body (soma) contains the nucleus and organelles that maintain the cell
The axon conducts electrical impulses away from the cell body toward the axon terminals
The myelin sheath, produced by Schwann cells (PNS) or oligodendrocytes (CNS), insulates axons and speeds signal conduction
Nodes of Ranvier are gaps in the myelin sheath where saltatory conduction allows the impulse to 'jump,' greatly increasing speed
Neuroglia (glial cells) support, protect, and nourish neurons but do not transmit impulses themselves

concepts.intro: An action potential is a rapid, temporary reversal of membrane voltage that allows neurons to transmit signals over long distances.
b: Resting membrane potential is about -70 mV, maintained by the sodium-potassium pump and selective membrane permeability
Depolarization occurs when voltage-gated sodium channels open, allowing Na+ to rush into the cell
Repolarization occurs when sodium channels close and voltage-gated potassium channels open, allowing K+ to exit
The action potential is 'all-or-none' — it either fires at full strength once threshold (~-55 mV) is reached, or it does not fire at all
The refractory period ensures the action potential travels in one direction and limits the maximum firing rate of a neuron

concepts.intro: Neurons communicate with each other and with effector cells across synapses, most commonly using chemical neurotransmitters.
b: An action potential reaching the axon terminal triggers voltage-gated calcium channels to open
Calcium influx causes synaptic vesicles to release neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft via exocytosis
Neurotransmitter binds receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, causing excitatory (depolarizing) or inhibitory (hyperpolarizing) effects
Common neurotransmitters include acetylcholine, dopamine, serotonin, norepinephrine, and GABA
Neurotransmitter is cleared from the synapse by reuptake, enzymatic breakdown, or diffusion, ending the signal

concepts.intro: The CNS, consisting of the brain and spinal cord, integrates sensory information and coordinates the body's responses.
b: The cerebrum, the largest brain region, is divided into frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital lobes, each with specialized functions
The cerebellum coordinates balance, posture, and fine motor movement
The brainstem (midbrain, pons, medulla oblongata) controls vital, automatic functions like heart rate and breathing
The hypothalamus regulates homeostasis (temperature, hunger, thirst) and links the nervous and endocrine systems via the pituitary gland
The spinal cord conducts signals between the brain and body and mediates reflexes independently of the brain
Meninges (dura mater, arachnoid mater, pia mater) and cerebrospinal fluid protect and cushion the CNS

concepts.intro: The PNS connects the CNS to the rest of the body and is divided into sensory and motor divisions with further subdivisions.
b: The sensory (afferent) division carries information from receptors toward the CNS
The motor (efferent) division carries commands from the CNS to muscles and glands
The somatic nervous system controls voluntary movement of skeletal muscle
The autonomic nervous system controls involuntary functions and is divided into sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions
The sympathetic division triggers 'fight-or-flight' responses (increased heart rate, dilated pupils, redirected blood flow)
The parasympathetic division promotes 'rest-and-digest' functions (decreased heart rate, increased digestion)

concepts.intro: Reflexes are rapid, automatic responses that protect the body, and disruptions to neural structures cause characteristic disorders.
b: A reflex arc includes a receptor, sensory neuron, integration center (often the spinal cord), motor neuron, and effector
The patellar (knee-jerk) reflex is a classic example of a monosynaptic reflex arc
Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune disease that destroys myelin in the CNS, slowing nerve conduction
Parkinson's disease results from the loss of dopamine-producing neurons, causing tremors and movement difficulty
Alzheimer's disease involves progressive neuron loss and is associated with amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles

keyFacts: The brain contains roughly 86 billion neurons, but far more glial cells supporting them
Saltatory conduction along myelinated axons can be up to 100 times faster than conduction along unmyelinated axons
The sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions typically have opposite effects on the same organs (antagonistic control)
The blood-brain barrier, formed by tight junctions in brain capillaries, restricts what substances can pass from blood into brain tissue
traps: Nerve impulses are electrical within the neuron but chemical between neurons at the synapse — not electrical the entire way
The action potential does NOT get bigger with a stronger stimulus — it is all-or-none; a stronger stimulus increases firing frequency, not amplitude
The sympathetic division does not 'turn off' the parasympathetic division and vice versa — both often act simultaneously with one usually dominating
Neuroglia (glial cells) are far more numerous than neurons in the brain, but they do not directly generate or transmit nerve impulses

units.name: Circulatory & Respiratory

concepts.l: Heart Structure and the Cardiac Cycle
concepts.intro: The heart is a four-chambered muscular pump that circulates blood through the body via a precisely coordinated sequence of contractions.
b: The heart has two atria (receiving chambers) and two ventricles (pumping chambers)
The right side pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs (pulmonary circuit); the left side pumps oxygenated blood to the body (systemic circuit)
Atrioventricular (AV) valves (tricuspid, mitral/bicuspid) prevent backflow from ventricles to atria
Semilunar valves (pulmonary, aortic) prevent backflow from arteries back into the ventricles
The cardiac cycle consists of systole (contraction) and diastole (relaxation) of the heart chambers
The left ventricle has the thickest wall because it must generate enough pressure to pump blood throughout the entire body

concepts.intro: The heart's rhythmic contraction is coordinated by a specialized electrical conduction system, allowing it to beat independently of the nervous system.
b: The sinoatrial (SA) node, located in the right atrium, is the heart's natural pacemaker
The electrical signal spreads through the atria, causing atrial contraction, then reaches the atrioventricular (AV) node
The AV node briefly delays the signal, allowing the atria to finish emptying before ventricular contraction
The signal travels down the Bundle of His and Purkinje fibers, triggering coordinated ventricular contraction
An electrocardiogram (ECG/EKG) records this electrical activity; the P wave, QRS complex, and T wave correspond to atrial depolarization, ventricular depolarization, and ventricular repolarization

concepts.intro: Blood travels through a closed system of vessels, and blood itself is a specialized connective tissue with distinct cellular and liquid components.
b: Arteries carry blood away from the heart and have thick, muscular, elastic walls to withstand high pressure
Veins carry blood toward the heart and contain valves to prevent backflow against gravity
Capillaries are single-cell-thick vessels where gas, nutrient, and waste exchange occurs
Blood consists of plasma (55%, mostly water) and formed elements (45%): red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets
Red blood cells (erythrocytes) contain hemoglobin, which binds and transports oxygen
White blood cells (leukocytes) fight infection; platelets (thrombocytes) are essential for blood clotting

concepts.intro: Blood type compatibility and the clotting cascade are critical clinical concepts governed by antigens on red blood cells and a cascade of clotting factors.
b: The ABO blood group system is based on A and B antigens present or absent on red blood cell surfaces
Type O negative is the universal donor; type AB positive is the universal recipient
The Rh factor (positive or negative) is an additional antigen that must be matched, especially important in pregnancy
Hemostasis (clot formation) involves vascular spasm, platelet plug formation, and the coagulation cascade producing a fibrin mesh
Vitamin K is required for the liver to synthesize several clotting factors

concepts.intro: The respiratory system moves air into and out of the lungs and provides the surface for gas exchange with the blood.
b: Air passes through the nasal cavity/pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, and into alveoli
The epiglottis prevents food from entering the trachea during swallowing
Alveoli are tiny air sacs surrounded by capillaries where gas exchange occurs across a thin respiratory membrane
Inhalation occurs when the diaphragm contracts and flattens, increasing thoracic volume and decreasing pressure, drawing air in
Exhalation is typically passive, occurring as the diaphragm relaxes and the elastic lungs recoil
Surfactant, produced by cells in the alveoli, reduces surface tension and prevents alveolar collapse

concepts.intro: Oxygen and carbon dioxide move by diffusion along pressure gradients, and disruptions to this system cause well-known respiratory and cardiovascular diseases.
b: External respiration: oxygen diffuses from alveoli into blood; carbon dioxide diffuses from blood into alveoli
Internal respiration: oxygen diffuses from blood into tissues; carbon dioxide diffuses from tissues into blood
Most oxygen is transported bound to hemoglobin; most carbon dioxide is transported as bicarbonate ions in plasma
The medulla oblongata controls the basic rhythm of breathing, primarily responding to blood CO2 (and pH) levels
Atherosclerosis (arterial plaque buildup) and hypertension increase the risk of heart attack and stroke
Asthma causes bronchiole constriction and inflammation; COPD (emphysema/chronic bronchitis) causes progressive, largely irreversible airflow limitation

keyFacts: The heart beats roughly 100,000 times per day, pumping about 5 liters of blood per minute at rest
The pulmonary artery is the only artery in the body that carries deoxygenated blood; the pulmonary vein is the only vein that carries oxygenated blood
Hemoglobin's affinity for carbon monoxide is over 200 times greater than for oxygen, making CO poisoning extremely dangerous
The SA node sets heart rate at rest (~60-100 bpm), but the autonomic nervous system and hormones like epinephrine can speed or slow it
traps: Arteries do not always carry oxygenated blood — the pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood to the lungs; it is direction (away from heart), not oxygen content, that defines an artery
The AV node does not initiate the heartbeat — the SA node is the primary pacemaker; the AV node only relays and delays the signal
Inhalation is active (requires diaphragm contraction); quiet exhalation is passive (elastic recoil), not muscular effort
Blood 'type O' still has antigens for the immune system to consider (the Rh factor) — 'universal donor' refers specifically to ABO/Rh compatibility, not total absence of all markers

units.name: Digestive & Excretory

concepts.intro: The digestive system is a long muscular tube (the alimentary canal) plus accessory organs that mechanically and chemically break down food for absorption.
b: The alimentary canal runs: mouth, pharynx, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, rectum, anus
Accessory organs (salivary glands, liver, gallbladder, pancreas) secrete substances into the canal but food does not pass through them
Peristalsis is the wave-like smooth muscle contraction that propels food through the digestive tract
Digestion includes both mechanical breakdown (chewing, churning) and chemical breakdown (enzymes)
The four layers of the GI tract wall, from innermost to outermost, are mucosa, submucosa, muscularis, and serosa

concepts.intro: Digestion begins in the mouth and continues through the esophagus into the stomach, where food is churned and chemically broken down.
b: Salivary amylase in saliva begins the chemical digestion of starches in the mouth
The esophagus uses peristalsis to move the food bolus to the stomach; the lower esophageal sphincter prevents reflux
The stomach secretes hydrochloric acid (HCl) and pepsinogen, which is activated to pepsin to begin protein digestion
Mucus-secreting cells protect the stomach lining from its own acidic, enzymatic environment
Food leaves the stomach as a semi-liquid mixture called chyme, released gradually into the small intestine via the pyloric sphincter

concepts.intro: Most chemical digestion and virtually all nutrient absorption occur in the small intestine, with essential help from the liver, gallbladder, and pancreas.
b: The small intestine has three sections: duodenum, jejunum, and ileum
Villi and microvilli dramatically increase the small intestine's surface area for nutrient absorption
The liver produces bile, which emulsifies (breaks up) fats to aid digestion by lipase
The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile, releasing it into the duodenum when fatty food is present
The pancreas secretes digestive enzymes (amylase, lipase, proteases) and bicarbonate to neutralize stomach acid entering the duodenum
The pancreas also has an endocrine role, producing insulin and glucagon from the islets of Langerhans

concepts.intro: The large intestine completes the digestive process by absorbing water and electrolytes and compacting waste for elimination.
b: The large intestine (colon) absorbs water and electrolytes from indigestible food matter
Beneficial gut bacteria in the colon synthesize some vitamins (like vitamin K) and ferment undigested material
Sections of the colon include the ascending, transverse, descending, and sigmoid colon, ending at the rectum and anus
Feces consist of indigestible fiber, bacteria, and water
The internal anal sphincter is involuntary; the external anal sphincter is under voluntary control

concepts.intro: The kidneys filter blood to remove wastes and regulate fluid and electrolyte balance through the functional unit called the nephron.
b: The nephron is the functional unit of the kidney, consisting of the glomerulus and renal tubule
Glomerular filtration: blood pressure forces water, ions, and small molecules from the glomerulus into Bowman's capsule
Tubular reabsorption: needed substances (glucose, water, ions) are reabsorbed from the filtrate back into the blood, mostly in the proximal convoluted tubule
Tubular secretion: additional wastes and excess ions are actively secreted from blood into the filtrate
The loop of Henle creates a concentration gradient in the kidney medulla that allows the kidney to concentrate urine
Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) increases water reabsorption in the collecting duct, concentrating urine when the body needs to conserve water

concepts.l: The Urinary System and Digestive/Excretory Disorders
concepts.intro: Beyond the kidneys, the urinary system stores and eliminates urine, and both systems are subject to well-known clinical conditions.
b: Urine travels from the kidneys through the ureters to the bladder, then out through the urethra
The kidneys also regulate blood pressure (via renin), blood pH, and red blood cell production (via erythropoietin)
Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) occurs when the lower esophageal sphincter fails to prevent stomach acid from entering the esophagus
Peptic ulcers are erosions in the stomach or duodenal lining, often caused by H. pylori infection or NSAID overuse
Kidney stones form when minerals crystallize in the urinary tract, and chronic kidney disease reflects progressive, often irreversible loss of nephron function

keyFacts: The small intestine is about 6 meters (20 feet) long and is the primary site of nutrient absorption due to its vast surface area from villi and microvilli
The liver is the body's largest internal organ and performs bile production, detoxification, and nutrient storage/processing
Each kidney contains roughly 1 million nephrons, and the kidneys filter the entire blood volume many times per day
Bile does not chemically digest fat; it physically emulsifies fat into smaller droplets so pancreatic lipase can act on it more efficiently
traps: The gallbladder does not produce bile — the liver produces bile; the gallbladder only stores and concentrates it
'Stomach acid digests protein' is incomplete — HCl activates pepsinogen into pepsin and denatures proteins, but pepsin (an enzyme) does the actual chemical digestion
Most nutrient absorption happens in the small intestine, not the large intestine — the large intestine mainly absorbs water and electrolytes
Urine is not simply filtered blood — it is the filtrate remaining after reabsorption of most water, glucose, and ions back into the blood

units.name: Endocrine & Immune

concepts.l: Endocrine System Overview and Hormone Action
concepts.intro: The endocrine system uses glands that secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream to regulate body processes slowly and over a long duration, in contrast to the fast, localized signals of the nervous system.
b: Hormones are chemical messengers released by endocrine glands that travel through the blood to act on distant target cells
Target cells respond to a hormone only if they have the matching receptor, either on the cell surface (peptide hormones) or inside the cell (steroid hormones)
Peptide/protein hormones (e.g., insulin) are water-soluble and bind surface receptors, triggering a second-messenger cascade
Steroid hormones (e.g., cortisol, testosterone, estrogen) are lipid-soluble, cross the cell membrane, and bind receptors inside the cell to directly affect gene expression
The hypothalamus links the nervous and endocrine systems by controlling the pituitary gland
Effects of hormones tend to be slower to start but longer-lasting than nerve impulses

concepts.intro: The pituitary gland, controlled by the hypothalamus, is often called the 'master gland' because it releases hormones that regulate other endocrine glands, including the thyroid.
b: The anterior pituitary secretes tropic hormones such as TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone), ACTH (adrenocorticotropic hormone), FSH, LH, and growth hormone (GH)
The posterior pituitary stores and releases two hormones made by the hypothalamus: antidiuretic hormone (ADH) and oxytocin
Growth hormone stimulates growth and cell reproduction; oversecretion in childhood causes gigantism, undersecretion causes pituitary dwarfism
The thyroid gland, in the neck, produces thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3), which set the body's basal metabolic rate
Thyroid hormone production requires dietary iodine; iodine deficiency can cause an enlarged thyroid (goiter)

Hypothyroidism (too little thyroid hormone) causes fatigue, weight gain, and cold intolerance; hyperthyroidism (too much, as in Graves' disease) causes weight loss, rapid heart rate, and heat intolerance

concepts.intro: The adrenal glands sit atop the kidneys and manage the body's stress response, while the pancreas manages blood sugar through two antagonistic hormones.
b: The adrenal medulla (inner region) releases epinephrine (adrenaline) and norepinephrine for the rapid 'fight-or-flight' response
The adrenal cortex (outer region) releases cortisol, a steroid hormone that raises blood glucose and suppresses the immune system during prolonged stress
The adrenal cortex also releases aldosterone, which increases sodium (and water) reabsorption in the kidneys to help regulate blood pressure
The pancreas is both an exocrine gland (digestive enzymes) and an endocrine gland (hormones from clusters of cells called the islets of Langerhans)
Beta cells of the pancreas secrete insulin, which lowers blood glucose by promoting its uptake into cells and storage as glycogen in the liver
Alpha cells secrete glucagon, which raises blood glucose by stimulating the breakdown of glycogen into glucose

concepts.intro: Most hormone levels are controlled by negative feedback loops that keep the body in a stable internal state (homeostasis) by counteracting change.
b: In negative feedback, a rise in a hormone or its effect suppresses further release of that hormone, keeping levels within a narrow range
Example: rising thyroid hormone (T3/T4) feeds back to inhibit the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary, reducing TRH and TSH release
Example: rising blood glucose triggers insulin release; falling blood glucose triggers glucagon release, so the two hormones oppose each other to keep glucose stable

Positive feedback loops amplify a change instead of reversing it and are rarer; oxytocin during childbirth is a classic example, where uterine contractions trigger more oxytocin release until delivery
Type 1 diabetes results from autoimmune destruction of insulin-producing beta cells, so blood glucose cannot be lowered normally
Type 2 diabetes results from cells becoming resistant to insulin's effects, often linked to obesity and lifestyle factors

concepts.intro: Innate immunity is the body's fast-acting, nonspecific defense system, active from birth, that responds the same way to any pathogen.
b: The first line of defense includes physical and chemical barriers: intact skin, mucous membranes, stomach acid, and enzymes in tears and saliva
The second line of defense activates once a pathogen breaches the first line, including phagocytic white blood cells, the inflammatory response, fever, and the complement system
Neutrophils are the most abundant white blood cell and are usually the first phagocytes to arrive at a site of infection
Macrophages engulf pathogens by phagocytosis and also display pieces of the pathogen (antigens) on their surface to alert the adaptive immune system
Natural killer (NK) cells patrol the body and destroy virus-infected and cancerous cells without needing to recognize a specific antigen
Inflammation (redness, heat, swelling, pain) increases blood flow and vessel permeability to bring immune cells to the injury site; fever raises body temperature to slow pathogen reproduction

concepts.intro: Adaptive immunity is slower to activate than innate immunity but is highly specific to a particular pathogen and creates lasting memory.
b: B lymphocytes (B cells) drive humoral immunity by differentiating into plasma cells that secrete antibodies specific to one antigen

T lymphocytes (T cells) drive cell-mediated immunity; helper T cells coordinate the immune response by activating B cells and cytotoxic T cells, while cytotoxic T cells directly destroy infected or abnormal cells
An antibody (immunoglobulin) is a Y-shaped protein that binds a specific antigen, marking it for destruction or neutralizing it directly
After an infection, some B and T cells become long-lived memory cells, allowing a faster, stronger secondary immune response if the same pathogen is encountered again
Active immunity develops when the body makes its own antibodies, either from natural infection or from vaccination with a weakened, inactivated, or partial pathogen/antigen
Passive immunity comes from receiving ready-made antibodies (e.g., from mother to infant across the placenta or in breast milk); it acts immediately but is temporary since no memory cells are formed

keyFacts: HIV specifically infects and destroys helper T cells, which is why it progressively cripples the ability to coordinate both humoral and cell-mediated immunity

The hypothalamus and pituitary form a control axis: the hypothalamus releases tropic hormones that tell the anterior pituitary which hormones to release, which in turn control glands like the thyroid, adrenal cortex, and gonads
Insulin and glucagon are antagonistic hormones from the same organ (the pancreas), a clear example of how negative feedback keeps blood glucose within a narrow range
A vaccine does not give a person the disease; it trains the immune system to produce memory cells so a real infection triggers a fast, strong secondary response
traps: Insulin lowers blood glucose and glucagon raises it, not the other way around — students frequently swap these two

The adrenal medulla releases epinephrine for short-term 'fight-or-flight' response, while the adrenal cortex releases cortisol for longer-term stress response — they are different regions with different hormones
Vaccination provides active immunity (the body makes its own antibodies and memory cells), not passive immunity — passive immunity comes from receiving pre-made antibodies and does not last
Innate immunity is fast but nonspecific and has no memory; adaptive immunity is slower to start but is pathogen-specific and creates memory cells for faster future responses

units.name: Reproductive & Homeostasis

concepts.intro: The male reproductive system is built to produce, mature, and deliver sperm, with testosterone driving both sperm production and male secondary sex characteristics.
b: The testes are the primary male reproductive organs, producing sperm (spermatogenesis) and the hormone testosterone
Sperm are produced in the seminiferous tubules inside the testes, then travel to the epididymis to mature and be stored
The vas deferens transports mature sperm from the epididymis toward the urethra during ejaculation
The seminal vesicles and prostate gland add fluid containing nutrients (like fructose) and buffers, which together with sperm make up semen
Testosterone, produced mainly by the testes, drives sperm production and the development of secondary sex characteristics such as facial hair and a deeper voice
Spermatogenesis is a continuous process that begins at puberty and produces millions of sperm daily throughout adult life

concepts.intro: The female reproductive system produces eggs, provides the site for fertilization, and supports a developing fetus if pregnancy occurs.
b: The ovaries are the primary female reproductive organs, producing eggs (oocytes) and the hormones estrogen and progesterone
Unlike sperm production, oogenesis begins before birth; a female is born with all the immature egg cells she will ever have
The fallopian tubes (oviducts) carry an egg from the ovary toward the uterus and are the usual site of fertilization
The uterus is a muscular organ lined by the endometrium, which thickens each cycle to potentially support a fertilized egg
The cervix is the narrow lower portion of the uterus that opens into the vagina, the muscular canal that receives sperm and serves as the birth canal
Only one egg is typically released per menstrual cycle (ovulation), compared to the continuous mass production of sperm in males

concepts.intro: The menstrual cycle is a roughly month-long hormonal cycle that prepares an egg for release and the uterus for possible pregnancy, driven by feedback between the pituitary and ovaries.
b: The cycle (about 28 days) has phases: the follicular phase, ovulation, the luteal phase, and menstruation
Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) from the anterior pituitary stimulates growth of an ovarian follicle containing the developing egg
The growing follicle secretes rising estrogen, which builds up the uterine endometrium and eventually triggers a surge of luteinizing hormone (LH)
The LH surge triggers ovulation, the release of the mature egg from the ovary, typically around day 14 of a 28-day cycle
After ovulation, the ruptured follicle becomes the corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone to maintain the endometrium in case of pregnancy
If fertilization does not occur, the corpus luteum degenerates, progesterone and estrogen drop, and the endometrium sheds as menstruation

concepts.intro: Fertilization combines genetic material from sperm and egg to form a new individual, which then undergoes early development and implants in the uterus.
b: Fertilization occurs when a sperm nucleus fuses with an egg nucleus, typically in the fallopian tube, forming a single-celled zygote
The zygote undergoes rapid cell division (cleavage) as it travels down the fallopian tube toward the uterus
By about day 5-6, the developing embryo forms a blastocyst, a hollow ball of cells, which implants into the endometrium
The placenta develops from both embryonic and maternal tissue, allowing exchange of gases, nutrients, and wastes between mother and fetus without their blood directly mixing
Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), produced by the developing placenta, maintains the corpus luteum early in pregnancy and is the hormone detected by pregnancy tests
Human development is divided into three trimesters, with major organ formation occurring in the first trimester

concepts.intro: Homeostasis is the body's maintenance of a stable internal environment despite external changes, achieved mainly through negative feedback loops.
b: Homeostasis relies on receptors (sensors that detect change), a control center (that compares the change to a set point), and effectors (that carry out a response)
In negative feedback, a deviation from the set point triggers a response that pushes the variable back toward the set point, which is the most common regulatory mechanism in the body
Positive feedback loops amplify a change rather than reversing it and are used only in specific processes, such as childbirth or blood clotting, because they must eventually be shut off
Blood glucose regulation by insulin and glucagon is a classic example of negative feedback maintaining homeostasis
Loss of homeostatic control, such as failure to regulate blood glucose or body temperature, can quickly become life-threatening

concepts.intro: Thermoregulation keeps body temperature within a narrow range, and osmoregulation keeps water and solute concentrations balanced; both are controlled by the hypothalamus using negative feedback.
b: The hypothalamus acts as the body's thermostat, comparing blood temperature to a set point (around 37°C/98.6°F in humans)
When body temperature rises, the hypothalamus triggers vasodilation (blood vessels widen to release heat) and sweating (evaporative cooling)
When body temperature falls, the hypothalamus triggers vasoconstriction (blood vessels narrow to conserve heat) and shivering (muscle contractions generate heat)
Osmoregulation is the control of water and solute balance, carried out mainly by the kidneys

Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect blood solute concentration; when blood becomes too concentrated (dehydration), the posterior pituitary releases more ADH, which increases water reabsorption in the kidneys
Aldosterone, from the adrenal cortex, increases sodium reabsorption in the kidneys, which indirectly promotes water retention and helps regulate blood pressure

keyFacts: A female is born with all the immature egg cells she will ever produce, while males continuously generate new sperm throughout adult life via spermatogenesis
The corpus luteum's progesterone output is essential to maintaining the uterine lining; if it degrades without a rescuing pregnancy hormone (hCG), menstruation follows
The placenta allows nutrient, gas, and waste exchange between mother and fetus but keeps their blood supplies separate — maternal and fetal blood do not normally mix
The hypothalamus is the shared control center for both thermoregulation (body temperature) and osmoregulation (water/solute balance), each managed through negative feedback
traps: Ovulation is triggered by a surge in luteinizing hormone (LH), not follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) — FSH's main job is stimulating follicle growth earlier in the cycle
Fertilization normally occurs in the fallopian tube, not the uterus — the uterus is where implantation of the resulting blastocyst happens several days later
Positive feedback amplifies a change (as in childbirth contractions), while negative feedback reverses it — most homeostatic regulation in the body relies on negative, not positive, feedback

Sweating and vasodilation are the body's responses to being too hot, while shivering and vasoconstriction respond to being too cold — students often mix up which response goes with which temperature direction

quiz.q: In standard anatomical position, which way do the palms face?
quiz.e: Anatomical position is defined with the palms facing forward (anteriorly).

quiz.q: Which term means 'toward the head'?
quiz.e: Superior means toward the head or upper part of the body.

quiz.q: The elbow is ___ to the wrist.
quiz.e: Proximal means closer to the point of attachment to the trunk; the elbow is closer to the trunk than the wrist.

quiz.q: Which plane divides the body into anterior and posterior portions?
quiz.e: The frontal, or coronal, plane splits the body into front and back sections.

quiz.q: A transverse plane divides the body into which sections?
quiz.e: The transverse plane is a horizontal cut separating upper (superior) from lower (inferior) body parts.

quiz.q: Which structure separates the thoracic cavity from the abdominopelvic cavity?
quiz.e: The diaphragm is the dome-shaped muscle separating the thoracic and abdominopelvic cavities.

quiz.q: The heart is located within which structure?
o: The pericardial cavity within the mediastinum
quiz.e: The heart sits in the pericardial cavity, part of the mediastinum in the thoracic cavity.

quiz.q: Which is the correct order of structural organization, from simplest to most complex?
quiz.e: Organization proceeds chemical, cellular, tissue, organ, organ system, organism.

quiz.q: Which tissue type is avascular and covers body surfaces?
quiz.e: Epithelial tissue lacks its own blood supply and forms coverings and linings.

quiz.q: Which tissue type includes blood, bone, and adipose tissue?
quiz.e: Connective tissue is a broad category that includes blood, bone, cartilage, and fat.

quiz.q: A negative feedback loop functions to:
o: Amplify a change until a threshold is reached
Reverse a change and restore the original set point
quiz.e: Negative feedback loops counteract a stimulus to return the body to its set point.

quiz.q: Which of the following is an example of a positive feedback loop?
o: Regulation of blood glucose by insulin
Uterine contractions during labor stimulated by oxytocin
Regulation of blood calcium by parathyroid hormone
quiz.e: Labor contractions are reinforced by oxytocin release in a self-amplifying positive feedback loop until birth occurs.

quiz.q: Which term describes a structure located away from the midline of the body?
quiz.e: Lateral means farther from the midline of the body.

quiz.q: Which cavity contains the brain?
quiz.e: The cranial cavity, part of the dorsal body cavity, houses the brain.

quiz.q: The three components of a feedback loop are the receptor, control center, and:
quiz.e: The effector is the structure that carries out the response directed by the control center.

quiz.q: Which plane, if positioned exactly down the midline, creates two mirror-image halves?
quiz.e: Only the midsagittal plane splits the body into equal left and right halves; other sagittal planes are off-center (parasagittal).

quiz.q: Which serous membrane lines the abdominal cavity and covers the abdominal organs?
quiz.e: The peritoneum is the serous membrane of the abdominopelvic cavity.

quiz.q: A parietal layer of a serous membrane is best described as:
o: Lining the wall of the cavity
Found only in the nervous system
quiz.e: The parietal layer lines the cavity wall, while the visceral layer covers the organ.

quiz.q: Physiology is best defined as the study of:
quiz.e: Physiology examines how body structures function, complementing anatomy's focus on structure.

quiz.q: Which region would contain the umbilicus in the 9-region abdominal division?
quiz.e: The umbilical region is the central region surrounding the navel.

quiz.q: Which directional term means 'near the surface of the body'?
quiz.e: Superficial refers to structures close to the body's surface.

quiz.q: The wrist is ___ to the elbow.
quiz.e: Distal means farther from the trunk; the wrist is farther from the trunk than the elbow.

quiz.q: Which of the four tissue types is responsible for generating and transmitting electrical impulses?
quiz.e: Nervous tissue, composed of neurons and neuroglia, generates and conducts electrical signals.

quiz.q: Which cavity houses the spinal cord?
quiz.e: The vertebral canal, part of the dorsal cavity, encloses and protects the spinal cord.

quiz.q: The mediastinum is located within which cavity?
quiz.e: The mediastinum is the central region of the thoracic cavity, containing the heart, esophagus, and trachea.

quiz.q: Which best distinguishes 'anterior' from 'ventral' in humans?
o: Anterior refers only to the head
quiz.e: In humans, anterior and ventral both mean toward the front of the body and are used interchangeably.

quiz.q: Which level of organization is represented by the stomach?
quiz.e: The stomach is an organ, composed of multiple tissue types working together.

quiz.q: A CT scan slice viewed as a 'cross-section' of the torso corresponds to which plane?
quiz.e: Standard CT/MRI cross-sectional images are taken along the transverse plane.

quiz.q: Which of the following pairs is mismatched?
quiz.e: Lateral means away from the midline; medial means toward the midline, so this pairing is incorrect.

quiz.q: Homeostasis refers to:
o: A relatively stable internal environment maintained despite external change
The four tissue types working together
quiz.e: Homeostasis is dynamic equilibrium, not perfectly constant conditions — the body maintains values within a narrow normal range.

quiz.q: Which structure would be considered 'deep' relative to the skin?
quiz.e: Skeletal muscle lies beneath the skin and superficial fascia, making it deep relative to the skin surface.

quiz.q: Which best describes the visceral layer of a serous membrane?
o: Covers the surface of the organ
quiz.e: The visceral layer directly covers the organ itself, as opposed to the parietal layer lining the cavity.

quiz.q: Which body cavity subdivision contains the urinary bladder and reproductive organs?
quiz.e: The pelvic cavity, part of the abdominopelvic cavity, houses the bladder and reproductive organs.

quiz.q: Epithelial tissue is characterized by all of the following EXCEPT:
quiz.e: Epithelial tissue is avascular; it receives nutrients by diffusion from underlying connective tissue.

quiz.q: Which term correctly describes the position of the heart relative to the sternum?
quiz.e: The heart lies deep to (behind) the sternum within the thoracic cavity.

quiz.q: An oblique section is best defined as a cut made:
o: At an angle between two standard planes
Parallel to the transverse plane only
quiz.e: Oblique sections are angled cuts that do not align with the standard sagittal, frontal, or transverse planes.

quiz.q: Which set point example illustrates negative feedback?
o: Fetal head pressing on the cervix during labor
quiz.e: Thermoregulation uses negative feedback to keep body temperature near a stable set point.

quiz.q: Which organ system pairing correctly matches the levels-of-organization concept?
o: Heart + blood vessels + blood = cardiovascular system
quiz.e: An organ system consists of multiple organs (heart, vessels) and tissues (blood) working toward a common function.

quiz.q: Which of the following is located in the axial region rather than the appendicular region?
quiz.e: The axial region includes the head, neck, and trunk (including the thorax); limbs are appendicular.

quiz.q: The term 'ipsilateral' refers to:
o: Structures on opposite sides of the body
Structures on the same side of the body
quiz.e: Ipsilateral describes structures located on the same side of the body.

quiz.q: How many bones are in the adult human skeleton?
quiz.e: The adult skeleton contains 206 bones, though infants have more that later fuse.

quiz.q: Which bone classification includes the femur and humerus?
quiz.e: Long bones have a shaft (diaphysis) and two ends (epiphyses), like the femur and humerus.

quiz.q: Which type of bone tissue forms the dense outer layer of bones?
quiz.e: Compact bone is the hard, dense tissue forming the outer shell of bones.

quiz.q: How many pairs of ribs make up the human rib cage?
quiz.e: There are 12 pairs of ribs, totaling 24 ribs.

quiz.q: Which ribs are classified as 'true ribs'?
quiz.e: True ribs (1-7) attach directly to the sternum via their own costal cartilage.

quiz.q: How many cervical vertebrae are there?
quiz.e: There are 7 cervical vertebrae in the neck region, regardless of body size.

quiz.q: Which bones make up the pectoral girdle?
quiz.e: The pectoral girdle consists of the clavicle (collarbone) and scapula (shoulder blade).

quiz.q: Which is the longest and strongest bone in the human body?
quiz.e: The femur, the thigh bone, is both the longest and strongest bone in the body.

quiz.q: Which joint type is completely immovable?
quiz.e: Fibrous joints, such as skull sutures, are synarthroses and allow no movement.

quiz.q: The shoulder and hip are examples of which synovial joint type?
quiz.e: Ball-and-socket joints allow the widest range of motion and are found at the shoulder and hip.

quiz.q: Which cells are responsible for building new bone matrix?
quiz.e: Osteoblasts synthesize and secrete new bone matrix (osteoid).

quiz.q: Which cells break down (resorb) bone tissue?
quiz.e: Osteoclasts resorb bone tissue, releasing calcium into the blood and allowing remodeling.

quiz.q: Longitudinal bone growth during childhood occurs at the:
quiz.e: The epiphyseal (growth) plate is the site of cartilage proliferation that lengthens long bones.

quiz.q: Which type of bone marrow is responsible for producing blood cells?
quiz.e: Red bone marrow contains hematopoietic stem cells that produce red and white blood cells and platelets.

quiz.q: Osteoporosis is best described as:
o: Decreased bone density increasing fracture risk
quiz.e: Osteoporosis is a reduction in bone mass/density that makes bones fragile and prone to fracture.

quiz.q: Vitamin D deficiency in children causing softened, weakened bones is called:
quiz.e: Rickets results from inadequate vitamin D, calcium, or phosphate, causing soft, deformed bones in children.

quiz.q: Which connective tissue attaches bone to bone at a joint?
quiz.e: Ligaments connect bone to bone and help stabilize joints.

quiz.q: Which connective tissue attaches muscle to bone?
quiz.e: Tendons connect skeletal muscle to bone, transmitting the force of contraction.

quiz.q: How many bones make up the human skull (cranial + facial)?
quiz.e: The skull has 8 cranial bones and 14 facial bones, totaling 22.

quiz.q: The atlas and axis are found in which region and allow which movement?
o: Cervical spine; rotation of the head
quiz.e: The atlas (C1) and axis (C2) form a pivot joint allowing rotational head movement, as in shaking your head 'no'.

quiz.q: Which best describes endochondral ossification?
o: Bone forms directly within a membrane
Bone forms on a hyaline cartilage model that is gradually replaced
Bone forms exclusively in flat bones
quiz.e: Endochondral ossification replaces a cartilage model with bone and is how most bones of the body form.

quiz.q: Which bones form via intramembranous ossification?
o: Flat bones of the skull and clavicle
quiz.e: Intramembranous ossification forms flat bones directly from mesenchymal (fibrous) tissue without a cartilage stage.

quiz.q: The pelvic girdle is formed by the fusion of which three bones?
quiz.e: The hip bone (os coxae) forms from the fusion of the ilium, ischium, and pubis.

quiz.q: Which stage of fracture repair occurs first?
quiz.e: A hematoma (blood clot) forms immediately at the fracture site, initiating the healing cascade.

quiz.q: Osteoarthritis primarily involves damage to which structure?
quiz.e: Osteoarthritis is the progressive breakdown of the articular cartilage cushioning joint surfaces.

quiz.q: Which joint allows movement in only one plane, like a door hinge?
quiz.e: Hinge joints, like the elbow and knee, permit flexion and extension in a single plane.

quiz.q: The saddle joint of the thumb is located at which articulation?
quiz.e: The carpometacarpal joint of the thumb is a saddle joint, allowing the thumb's unique opposition movement.

quiz.q: How many lumbar vertebrae are there?
quiz.e: There are 5 lumbar vertebrae, the largest of the movable vertebrae, in the lower back.

quiz.q: Which bone is unique in that it does not directly articulate with any other bone?
quiz.e: The hyoid bone in the neck is suspended by muscles and ligaments and does not form a joint with another bone.

quiz.q: Cartilage differs from bone primarily in that cartilage:
quiz.e: Cartilage is avascular, receiving nutrients by diffusion, unlike highly vascularized bone.

quiz.q: The pubic symphysis is an example of which joint type?
quiz.e: The pubic symphysis is a cartilaginous joint (amphiarthrosis) allowing slight movement.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a function of the skeletal system?
quiz.e: Bones store minerals, especially calcium and phosphorus, releasing them into the blood as needed.

quiz.q: Scoliosis refers to:
o: Abnormal lateral curvature of the spine
Softening of bones from vitamin D deficiency
quiz.e: Scoliosis is a sideways curvature of the vertebral column, often diagnosed in adolescence.

quiz.q: Synovial fluid, found within the joint capsule, primarily functions to:
o: Lubricate the joint and reduce friction
quiz.e: Synovial fluid lubricates the joint cavity, nourishes cartilage, and reduces friction during movement.

quiz.q: Which region of a long bone contains yellow marrow in adults?
quiz.e: The medullary cavity of the diaphysis stores yellow (fatty) marrow in adults.

quiz.q: The radius and ulna are bones of the:
quiz.e: The radius and ulna are the two bones of the forearm.

quiz.q: Which best describes 'false ribs' (ribs 8-10)?
o: They have no cartilage at all
They attach indirectly to the sternum via the cartilage of rib 7
They float freely with no anterior attachment
They are fused to the vertebrae only
quiz.e: False ribs 8-10 connect to the sternum indirectly through the costal cartilage of rib 7.

quiz.q: Floating ribs refer to ribs:
quiz.e: Ribs 11 and 12 have no anterior attachment to the sternum and are called floating ribs.

quiz.q: The periosteum is best described as:
o: A dense connective tissue membrane covering the outer bone surface
A type of cartilage found at joints
The site of red blood cell filtration
quiz.e: The periosteum is the fibrous membrane covering the outer surface of bone, providing attachment for tendons and containing blood vessels and nerve fibers.

quiz.q: Which vertebral region has vertebrae fused into a single bone in adults?
quiz.e: The 5 sacral vertebrae fuse into a single sacrum bone by adulthood.

quiz.q: Which type of muscle tissue is voluntary and striated?
quiz.e: Skeletal muscle is the only voluntary muscle type and appears striated under a microscope.

quiz.q: Intercalated discs are a distinguishing feature of which muscle type?
o: Visceral muscle only in the gut
quiz.e: Intercalated discs join cardiac muscle cells and contain gap junctions for rapid signal spread.

quiz.q: Which muscle tissue lines the walls of the intestines and blood vessels?
quiz.e: Smooth muscle is non-striated, involuntary, and found in the walls of hollow organs and vessels.

quiz.q: The basic contractile unit of skeletal muscle is the:
quiz.e: The sarcomere, bounded by Z-discs, is the smallest functional contractile unit of muscle.

quiz.q: Thick filaments in a sarcomere are composed of which protein?
quiz.e: Thick filaments are made of myosin, which forms cross-bridges with actin during contraction.

quiz.q: Which structure stores calcium ions needed for muscle contraction?
quiz.e: The sarcoplasmic reticulum is a specialized endoplasmic reticulum that stores and releases calcium.

quiz.q: Calcium ions trigger contraction by binding to which protein?
quiz.e: Calcium binds troponin, causing tropomyosin to shift and expose the myosin-binding sites on actin.

quiz.q: What neurotransmitter is released at the neuromuscular junction to trigger contraction?
quiz.e: Acetylcholine (ACh) released from motor neurons binds receptors on the muscle fiber, triggering depolarization.

quiz.q: What is required for the myosin head to detach from actin after the power stroke?
quiz.e: ATP binding to the myosin head is necessary to break the actin-myosin cross-bridge.

quiz.q: During muscle contraction, which band of the sarcomere stays the same length?
quiz.e: The A band, corresponding to the length of the thick (myosin) filaments, does not change length during contraction.

quiz.q: Which energy system provides the most immediate ATP for very short bursts of intense activity?
quiz.e: The phosphocreatine system rapidly regenerates ATP for about the first 10-15 seconds of intense exercise.

quiz.q: Which byproduct accumulates during anaerobic glycolysis and contributes to muscle fatigue?
quiz.e: Anaerobic glycolysis produces lactic acid when oxygen is insufficient for full aerobic metabolism.

quiz.q: Slow-twitch (Type I) muscle fibers are best characterized by:
o: Rapid fatigue and high power output
Fatigue resistance and reliance on aerobic metabolism
quiz.e: Type I fibers are fatigue-resistant, mitochondria-rich, and suited for endurance activity.

quiz.q: The muscle primarily responsible for producing a movement is called the:
quiz.e: The prime mover, or agonist, is the main muscle generating a given movement.

quiz.q: A muscle that opposes or reverses the action of the prime mover is the:
quiz.e: The antagonist muscle produces the opposite action of the agonist, such as the triceps opposing the biceps.

quiz.q: The fixed attachment point of a muscle that does not move during contraction is the:
quiz.e: The origin is the stable attachment point, while the insertion moves toward the origin during contraction.

quiz.q: An eccentric contraction is best described as:
o: Muscle generates tension with no length change
quiz.e: Eccentric contractions occur as the muscle lengthens under tension, such as lowering a weight slowly.

quiz.q: An isometric contraction is characterized by:
o: A change in muscle length with tension
Tension generated without a change in muscle length
quiz.e: Isometric contractions produce force without shortening or lengthening the muscle, as in holding a plank.

quiz.q: Which muscle is the primary muscle of respiration?
quiz.e: The diaphragm's contraction and relaxation drives the pressure changes that produce inhalation and exhalation.

quiz.q: Which muscle group extends the knee?
quiz.e: The quadriceps femoris group extends the knee, opposing the hamstrings which flex it.

quiz.q: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disease that attacks:
o: Acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction
quiz.e: In myasthenia gravis, antibodies attack acetylcholine receptors, impairing neuromuscular signal transmission and causing weakness.

quiz.q: Rigor mortis (stiffening of muscles after death) occurs primarily because:
o: Excess calcium enters cells with no ATP available to release cross-bridges
Muscles are still receiving nerve signals
quiz.e: After death, calcium leaks into the cytoplasm but ATP production stops, so myosin cannot detach from actin, locking muscles in contraction.

quiz.q: Which connective tissue wrapping surrounds an entire skeletal muscle?
quiz.e: The epimysium is the outermost connective tissue layer surrounding a whole muscle.

quiz.q: Which connective tissue wrapping surrounds individual muscle fibers?
quiz.e: The endomysium surrounds each individual muscle fiber (cell).

quiz.q: A fascicle is best described as:
quiz.e: A fascicle is a bundle of muscle fibers wrapped by the perimysium.

quiz.q: Which term describes muscle naming based on the number of origins, as in biceps brachii?
quiz.e: The prefix 'bi-' in biceps indicates the muscle has two heads (origins).

quiz.q: Muscular dystrophy refers to:
o: A group of genetic disorders causing progressive muscle degeneration
An autoimmune attack on acetylcholine receptors
A bacterial infection of muscle tissue
quiz.e: Muscular dystrophy encompasses inherited disorders that progressively weaken and break down skeletal muscle.

quiz.q: Muscle tone refers to:
o: Maximum strength a muscle can generate
A constant, low-level partial contraction of muscle at rest
quiz.e: Muscle tone is the baseline, sustained partial contraction that keeps muscles firm and ready to act, even at rest.

quiz.q: Which best describes a synergist muscle?
o: It assists the prime mover in producing a movement
It is always the largest muscle in a group
It only functions in smooth muscle
quiz.e: Synergists work alongside the prime mover to assist or fine-tune a movement.

quiz.q: A fixator muscle functions to:
o: Stabilize the origin bone so the prime mover can act effectively
quiz.e: Fixators stabilize a joint or bone, providing a stable base for the prime mover to pull against.

quiz.q: The deltoid muscle is named for its:
quiz.e: 'Deltoid' refers to its triangular (delta-shaped) form covering the shoulder.

quiz.q: Which pair of muscles produces flexion and extension at the elbow, respectively?
quiz.e: The biceps brachii flexes the elbow; the triceps brachii, its antagonist, extends it.

quiz.q: Excitation-contraction coupling refers to the process linking:
o: A nerve impulse to the physical contraction of a muscle fiber
quiz.e: Excitation-contraction coupling describes how an electrical signal (excitation) triggers calcium release and physical contraction.

quiz.q: Which muscle plantarflexes the foot (points the toes down)?
quiz.e: The gastrocnemius, the major calf muscle, plantarflexes the foot at the ankle.

quiz.q: Aerobic respiration is most heavily relied upon during:
o: The first 10 seconds of a sprint
Sustained, lower-intensity activity like distance running
quiz.e: Aerobic respiration, requiring oxygen, provides efficient, sustained ATP production for endurance activities.

quiz.q: The T-tubules (transverse tubules) function to:
o: Carry the electrical impulse deep into the muscle fiber to trigger calcium release
quiz.e: T-tubules are extensions of the sarcolemma that conduct the action potential into the cell's interior near the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

quiz.q: Which best distinguishes cardiac muscle from skeletal muscle?
o: Cardiac muscle is autorhythmic and does not require external nerve stimulation to contract
quiz.e: Cardiac muscle can generate its own rhythmic contractions (autorhythmicity) via the heart's pacemaker cells, unlike skeletal muscle.

quiz.q: Fast-twitch (Type II) fibers are best suited for:
o: Short bursts of powerful activity like sprinting or jumping
quiz.e: Fast-twitch fibers generate high force quickly but fatigue rapidly, ideal for explosive, short-duration activity.

quiz.q: The sarcolemma refers to the:
o: Plasma membrane of a muscle fiber
quiz.e: The sarcolemma is the specialized cell membrane surrounding a skeletal muscle fiber.

quiz.q: Tetanus, as a physiological term (not the disease), refers to:
o: A sustained, smooth contraction from high-frequency stimulation with no relaxation between stimuli
quiz.e: Physiological tetanus occurs when stimulation frequency is so high that individual twitches fuse into one sustained, maximal contraction.

quiz.q: Which part of the neuron receives incoming signals?
quiz.e: Dendrites receive signals from other neurons and conduct them toward the cell body.

quiz.q: Which structure conducts impulses away from the neuron cell body?
quiz.e: The axon carries the action potential away from the cell body toward the axon terminals.

quiz.q: Myelin sheaths in the peripheral nervous system are produced by:
quiz.e: Schwann cells myelinate axons in the PNS, while oligodendrocytes perform this role in the CNS.

quiz.q: Gaps in the myelin sheath where saltatory conduction occurs are called:
quiz.e: Nodes of Ranvier are unmyelinated gaps that allow the action potential to jump rapidly along the axon.

quiz.q: The resting membrane potential of a typical neuron is approximately:
quiz.e: A neuron at rest maintains a membrane potential of roughly -70 mV, negative inside relative to outside.

quiz.q: Depolarization of a neuron's membrane occurs due to the influx of which ion?
quiz.e: Voltage-gated sodium channels open during depolarization, allowing Na+ to rush into the cell.

quiz.q: Repolarization of the neuron membrane is primarily driven by the efflux of which ion?
quiz.e: Potassium channels open during repolarization, allowing K+ to exit and restore the negative resting potential.

quiz.q: The 'all-or-none' principle of the action potential means:
o: Stronger stimuli produce larger action potentials
An action potential either fires at full strength or does not fire at all
Action potentials only occur in the brain
Weak stimuli produce partial depolarization that still propagates
quiz.e: Once threshold is reached, the action potential always fires at the same magnitude, regardless of stimulus strength beyond threshold.

quiz.q: Which pump helps maintain the resting membrane potential by moving ions against their gradients?
quiz.e: The sodium-potassium pump actively transports 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in per ATP used, maintaining ion gradients.

quiz.q: At a chemical synapse, what triggers neurotransmitter release from the presynaptic neuron?
o: Calcium influx into the axon terminal
quiz.e: Calcium influx through voltage-gated channels at the axon terminal triggers synaptic vesicle exocytosis.

quiz.q: Which neurotransmitter is released at the neuromuscular junction?
quiz.e: Acetylcholine is the neurotransmitter used at neuromuscular junctions to stimulate skeletal muscle.

quiz.q: GABA is best described as a(n):
quiz.e: GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) is the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS, reducing neuron firing.

quiz.q: Which brain region is primarily responsible for coordinating balance and fine motor movement?
quiz.e: The cerebellum fine-tunes movement and maintains balance and posture.

quiz.q: Which brain structure regulates body temperature, hunger, and thirst?
quiz.e: The hypothalamus is the primary homeostatic control center, linking the nervous and endocrine systems.

quiz.q: Vital, automatic functions like heart rate and breathing are controlled by the:
quiz.e: The brainstem, including the medulla oblongata, regulates essential autonomic functions like heart rate and respiration.

quiz.q: Which lobe of the cerebrum is primarily responsible for processing visual information?
quiz.e: The occipital lobe, at the back of the brain, contains the primary visual cortex.

quiz.q: Which lobe is associated with reasoning, planning, and voluntary motor control?
quiz.e: The frontal lobe houses the primary motor cortex and areas for executive function, reasoning, and planning.

quiz.q: Which meningeal layer is the toughest, outermost layer surrounding the brain and spinal cord?
quiz.e: The dura mater is the thick, durable outermost meningeal layer.

quiz.q: The somatic nervous system controls:
quiz.e: The somatic division of the PNS governs conscious, voluntary control of skeletal muscles.

quiz.q: The autonomic nervous system is divided into which two divisions?
quiz.e: The autonomic nervous system has sympathetic (fight-or-flight) and parasympathetic (rest-and-digest) divisions.

quiz.q: Which division of the autonomic nervous system is responsible for the 'fight-or-flight' response?
quiz.e: The sympathetic division prepares the body for emergency action by increasing heart rate and redirecting blood flow to muscles.

quiz.q: Which division of the autonomic nervous system promotes digestion and lowers heart rate?
quiz.e: The parasympathetic division supports 'rest-and-digest' activities, conserving energy and promoting digestion.

quiz.q: A reflex arc's integration center, where the sensory signal connects to a motor response, is typically located in the:
quiz.e: Most simple reflex arcs are integrated in the spinal cord, allowing a rapid response without waiting for the brain.

quiz.q: The patellar (knee-jerk) reflex is an example of which type of reflex arc?
quiz.e: The patellar reflex involves a single synapse between the sensory and motor neuron, making it monosynaptic.

quiz.q: Multiple sclerosis is caused by damage to which structure?
quiz.e: MS is an autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks and destroys myelin in the central nervous system.

quiz.q: Parkinson's disease results primarily from the degeneration of neurons that produce:
quiz.e: Parkinson's disease is characterized by the loss of dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra.

quiz.q: Alzheimer's disease is associated with which pathological features?
quiz.e: Alzheimer's disease features amyloid-beta plaques and tau protein neurofibrillary tangles that disrupt neuron function.

quiz.q: The refractory period of a neuron functions to:
o: Increase the amplitude of the next action potential
Ensure unidirectional propagation and limit maximum firing rate
quiz.e: The refractory period prevents the action potential from traveling backward and caps how frequently a neuron can fire.

quiz.q: Neuroglia (glial cells) primarily function to:
quiz.e: Glial cells provide structural and metabolic support for neurons but do not typically transmit impulses themselves.

quiz.q: The blood-brain barrier is formed primarily by:
o: Tight junctions between capillary endothelial cells in the brain
quiz.e: Tight junctions between endothelial cells of brain capillaries restrict the passage of many substances from blood to brain tissue.

quiz.q: Cerebrospinal fluid functions to:
o: Cushion the brain and spinal cord and remove waste
quiz.e: CSF cushions the CNS against shock, provides buoyancy, and helps circulate nutrients and remove metabolic waste.

quiz.q: An afferent (sensory) neuron carries signals:
quiz.e: Afferent neurons carry sensory information from peripheral receptors toward the central nervous system.

quiz.q: An efferent (motor) neuron carries signals:
o: From the CNS to effectors (muscles and glands)
Only between neurons in the brain
From the eye to the optic nerve exclusively
quiz.e: Efferent neurons carry motor commands from the CNS out to muscles and glands.

quiz.q: Which structure in the brain connects the two cerebral hemispheres?
quiz.e: The corpus callosum is the thick band of nerve fibers connecting the left and right cerebral hemispheres.

quiz.q: Threshold potential refers to:
o: The resting potential of a neuron
The minimum depolarization needed to trigger an action potential
The maximum potential a neuron can reach
quiz.e: Threshold is the critical voltage level that, once reached, guarantees an action potential fires.

quiz.q: Which of the following best distinguishes the CNS from the PNS?
o: The CNS includes only sensory neurons
The CNS consists of the brain and spinal cord; the PNS includes all nerves outside them
The PNS controls involuntary functions exclusively
quiz.e: The CNS is the brain and spinal cord, while the PNS comprises the nerves and ganglia outside the CNS.

quiz.q: Saltatory conduction is faster than continuous conduction because the impulse:
o: Travels through the cell body first
Jumps from node to node along the myelinated axon
quiz.e: In saltatory conduction, the action potential 'jumps' between nodes of Ranvier, speeding transmission along myelinated axons.

quiz.q: Which term describes a neurotransmitter's effect that makes a postsynaptic neuron less likely to fire?
quiz.e: Inhibitory neurotransmitters, like GABA, hyperpolarize the postsynaptic membrane, making an action potential less likely.

quiz.q: The temporal lobe of the cerebrum is primarily associated with:
quiz.e: The temporal lobe contains the primary auditory cortex and is involved in processing sound and language.

quiz.q: Neurotransmitter is cleared from the synaptic cleft by all of the following EXCEPT:
o: Simple diffusion away from the synapse
quiz.e: Neurotransmitter is cleared via reuptake, enzymatic degradation, or diffusion — not by being converted into myelin.

quiz.q: Which heart chambers are primarily responsible for pumping blood out of the heart?
quiz.e: The ventricles are the heart's main pumping chambers, generating the force to send blood into the arteries.

quiz.q: The left ventricle has a thicker wall than the right ventricle because it:
o: Pumps blood only to the lungs
Must generate enough pressure to pump blood through the entire systemic circuit
quiz.e: The left ventricle needs greater force to push blood throughout the whole body, requiring thicker, more muscular walls.

quiz.q: Which valve prevents backflow from the left ventricle into the left atrium?
quiz.e: The mitral (bicuspid) valve sits between the left atrium and left ventricle, preventing backflow during ventricular contraction.

quiz.q: The heart's natural pacemaker is the:
quiz.e: The sinoatrial (SA) node in the right atrium initiates the electrical signal that sets the heart's rhythm.

quiz.q: The AV node's brief delay in conducting the electrical signal serves to:
o: Allow the atria to finish emptying before the ventricles contract
Produce the T wave on an ECG
quiz.e: The AV node delay ensures atrial contraction completes before ventricular contraction begins, optimizing filling.

quiz.q: On an ECG, the QRS complex corresponds to:
quiz.e: The QRS complex represents the electrical depolarization of the ventricles, triggering their contraction.
